newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany, France look to make up at Friday summit.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France look to make up at Friday summit.

text.p: France's divided leaders and Germany's weakened goverment hope to reach a deal on Europe's planned stability pact on Friday to ensure a successful European Union summit next week, officials in both countries said.

The stability pact, a code of fiscal discipline due to give Europe's single currency a heavy German accent, will top the agenda at the six-monthly consultation of the EU's core alliance in the western French city of Poitiers.

But Chancellor Helmut Kohl, suddenly no longer Europe's undisputed giant after the French election and his bungled scheme to revalue central bank gold, will have to let more Gallic tones join the chorus to ensure the single currency, his dream project, stays on track.

It will be Kohl's first meeting with Socialist French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who won an upset election victory on June 1 arguing that Europe must focus on growth and jobs, instead of austerity, to make the single currency acceptable to citizens.

The trick in Poitiers will be to find a formula that gives France some concession on fighting unemployment but will not cost German taxpayers more money. Commentator Josef Joffe remarked in Munich's Sueddeutsche Zeitung this meant a weaker euro or a rise in "the growing hypocrisy quotient in Europe".
Both German and French officials stressed they wanted a harmonious meeting, which will be Kohl's first with the new power-sharing duo of conservative President Jacques Chirac and Jospin.
"I'm sure we'll agree with France on the stability pact, so I think we don't have to be so worried about that," said German negotiator Werner Hoyer.

"This first contact between the Germans and the new French government team must...show the continuity of Franco-German relations, which are indispensible to the cause of European integration," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.

Bowing to the EU's new leftward lean following the British and French elections, Bonn agreed on Wednesday to add a jobs chapter to the revised Maastricht treaty on closer European union, due to be approved at the EU summit in Amsterdam next week.
German officials said they were still considering an extra jobs resolution to be added to the stability pact, which France says it cannot sign in its present form.

One Bonn source said an idea already proposed and rejected would have allowed countries to overshoot a public deficit level of three percent of GDP, the target to qualify for the single currency, if the extra borrowing was used to boost employment.
That was too Keynesian for Kohl's centre-right government.
Another official in Bonn said there would have to be some substance in the Amsterdam agreement, adding Jospin could not be given only a "fig-leaf resolution" to take back to Paris.

Both EU Commission President Jacques Santer and Prime Minister Wim Kok of the Netherlands, the current EU president, have been visiting EU states in a frantic search for a solution before Monday's Amsterdam summit.

The Jospin government stunned Bonn on Monday by asking for a delay to study the stability pact. The French left sees it as a monetary straitjacket that runs counter to the greater political influence they want to see on EU policy.
French officials said the new government was in a stronger bargaining position vis-a-vis Germany, which one said "was not in a position to pound its fist on the table".
But Pierre Lellouche, an adviser to Chirac and member of parliament for the defeated Gaullist party, said France must not press its case so far that it endangers economic and monetary union.

"Don't forget a big majority of the German public doesn't want a single currency, so if we give the impression of having doubts, it won't happen," he told LCI television. "Let's be careful not to play too much this balancing act between election promises and France's international commitments."
